utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we will hear the testimony of the first Chamber witness, the Chamber would briefly like to put a few matters on the record. For the sake of full transparency, the Chamber wishes to put on the record the steps taken by the Chamber with regard to the calling of Witness CW-1, which is Mr. Radic. As the parties recall, the Chamber announced its decision to call this witness on the 20th of January, and on the 28th of January, a legal officer of the Chamber contacted Witness Radic by phone and informed him about the Chamber's decision and about the possible date for testimony. This phone conversation was recorded with the knowledge of the witness, and may be provided to the parties, should any dispute arise as to what was said during the conversation. Subsequent to this, the Victims and Witness Section of the Registry contacted the witness on numerous occasions in order to make the practical arrangements with regard to the witness's travel to and stay in The Hague. On the 2nd of February, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's request to send Requests for Assistance to Croatia for Witness Radic and to the extent that the Request for Assistance did not require -- and to the extent that the RFA did not require Croatia to contact the witness regarding the substance of his testimony. I would like further to put on the record what is found in an e-mail of the 12th of February, 2010, in relation to the scope of cross-examination in general. Easiest is to just slowly read the substance of this e-mail. It reads: "Dear parties, on 27th of January, 2010, the Chamber informed the parties of its inclination to focus its examination-in-chief of the seven Chamber witnesses on very specific matters, and that the parties should also focus their cross-examinations on the matters raised in the examination-in-chief," which, is found at transcript page 27.106. "The parties were then invited by the Chamber to file written submissions by the 5th of February, 2010, should they fundamentally disagree with this approach." Same page of the transcript. "On the 5th of February, 2010, the Prosecution filed the Prosecution's submission on the scope of cross-examination of Chambers witnesses, in which it requested the Chamber to confirm that the scope of cross-examination includes the witnesses' credibility and to allow the parties to make requests in advance of the witnesses' testimony to extend the scope of cross-examination. "With regard to the first issue, the Chamber confirms that the scope of the cross-examination of Chamber witnesses will include their credibility. When cross-examining a Chamber witness, the parties will be able to read into the record portions of previous statements alleged to be inconsistent with any evidence given by the witness during his testimony in order to challenge the witness's credibility. "With regard to the second issue, the Chamber recalls that the rationale of Rule 90(H)(i) of the Rules, coupled with the fact that none of the parties called any of the Chamber witnesses during their cases, militates in favour of restricting cross-examination to the topics dealt with during the examination-in-chief. However, should the parties feel the need to extend the scope of their cross-examination, they shall make such requests as soon as possible." And then the e-mail continues to say that this will be put on the record, but I have read the substance of the e-mail of the 12th of February. Next item deals with the scope of the examination-in-chief of Chamber witness number 1. And the Chamber wants to put on the record that, on the 12th of February, 2010, the Trial Chamber informed the parties by e-mail of the intended scope of examination-in-chief of this witness. More specifically, that the Chamber intended to question Witness Radic with a view to exploring the consistency or inconsistency of the aims and purposes of the use of Croatia's governmental powers and instruments as expressed and observed in a public setting, on the one hand, and as found in non-public -- in a non-public setting on the other. Further, the Chamber would primarily focus on the following subject matters: The return of persons; the temporary takeover and reconstruction of property; and the security issues following Operation Storm. As far as the non-public setting is concerned, the Chamber would focus primarily on the Presidential and VONS meetings that the witness attended. As far as the public use of Croatia's governmental powers and instruments is concerned, the Chamber is not intending to seek any further evidence on legislative activities or on planning, developing, or implementing programmes on which the Chamber has already received extensive evidence by -- through witnesses, such as Witnesses Sterc, Skare Ozbolt, Skegro, and Bagic. The Prosecution has asked to give time-limits. The Chamber is not intending to put very strict time-limits but the Chamber expects that the testimony could be concluded in two days. And as the parties may be aware, we have swapped tomorrow's afternoon session to the morning session. However, if that would be not sufficient, then we still have Friday reserved to continue. Then I would like to move briefly into private session on a matter not directly related to this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. One preliminary matter before we ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom. In preparing for the first Chamber's witness, the Chamber received from the parties a statement that the witness gave to the Gotovina Defence, a statement which was signed on the 25th of May, 2009. This statement is not in evidence. However, if the Chamber would like to rely on that, it has requested it to be uploaded so that we can see it on our screens and if there's any need to put anything of his statement to the witness. Then, unless there are any questions in relation to these, I would say, preliminary matters, if there are, I would like to hear them; if not, we will ask the witness to be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President, procedurally. We filed an e-mail message to Chambers and parties yesterday concerning the order of examination by the parties when the Chamber concludes. We went and researched what the Chamber proposed and did in prior proceedings, and frankly, adopted that, in that the order of proceeding would be Prosecution with the burden of proof, then by the respective parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what was on the mind of the Chamber, and the Chamber was informed that the witness has shown some interest in knowing as well on how we would proceed. The one thing I do not know yet is whether a sequence of examination or cross-examination, whatever would you like to call it, I think we called it cross-examination among the Defence teams, whether that has been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I haven't discussed it with my colleagues. I certainly at the first break will do so. I thought, maybe presumptuously, that we would go first, as we have done in the past, and we are prepared to do so. So that's -- but I will talk to my colleagues on the break, and ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think we're at the point where we can ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Madam Usher. I also inform the parties that the Chamber has verified whether the witness would require any protective measures. The answer is that he didn't ask for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the Chamber was informed that you would very much like to know what the sequence of questioning will be. First, the Chamber will ask you questions. That might take quite some time. Once we have heard your testimony, the Prosecution will ask questions, and after that, the Defence counsel will ask questions. If there would be any need for further questions, we'll establish that once we have concluded these series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, would you please state your full name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: My name is Jure Radic. I was born on September 15, 1953.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic, I'll just first like to go through some general information. From 1992 to 1994, you were the Chief of Staff of the Office of the President of the Republic of Croatia and Secretary-General of the Defence and National Security Council, the VONS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. In early 1992, I was the minister for science, and then from mid-1992 up until the end of 1994, I was the head of the Office of the President and the Secretary-General of the VONS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were you deputy prime minister of the government of the Republic of Croatia and the minister of reconstruction and development from 1994 to 2000?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Since 1994, up until 2000, I was the vice-president of the Croatian government and the minister for reconstruction and development. But in the latter part of that period, there was another function added to the ministry so the name changed, and I actually became the minister for reconstruction, development, and relocation -- resettlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as a deputy prime minister and minister of reconstruction and development, and, as you said, later on, changed its name, were you closely involved in all tasks in the process of reconstruction, development, and the return of displaced persons following Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. My task was reconstruction of homes, of infrastructure and the conditions, living conditions, and enabling or making the conditions such that people can actually return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would now to move into a different area and deal with some of the meetings you were reported as having attended. Could we please pull up P462? Page 16 in the English and page 25 in the B/C/S. If you would like to look at the documents in hard copy and not only on your screen, we have prepared a binder which would enable to you look at the hard copies, but we'll start with having them on the screen. If have you any difficulties in reading them, please tell us. The front page, the first page of this document, mentions you as being present at this meeting on the 11th of August, 1995. Were you present?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I would have to read the details of the meeting. But it's quite possible and very likely that I was. A lot of time has passed in the meantime, but I could say that I attended most of the meetings that dealt with reconstruction and development so I do believe that I was present there, because my name is -- appears there. But once I see the context, I will probably refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If at any moment any doubts would come up as to your presence, we'd like to hear from you. Could I take to you page 25 in the B/C/S, page 16 in English. For the parties, when I'm referring to pages, I'm referring to e-court pages which are not necessarily the same as the pages -- as the paging as we find it in the document. Mr. Radic, from these minutes, the Chamber sees that you are recorded as having said, and I quote part of which is seen on your screen. You are reported to have said: "That Vojnic used to have only 51 inhabitants." You follow that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Today it's a town of 15.000 people. Tomorrow we can fill it up with 15.000 in addition. Lapac has 14 inhabitants, 14 Croats, Donji Lapac 14 inhabitants. (It's more than the number of houses)." Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I sincerely apologise for the interruption, Your Honours, but there is a -- I now notice translation errors in this paragraph so I don't know if you wish to tell me -- tell you outside the presence of the witness, but what the numbers are today versus used to be are mixed up in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, do you speak and understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can understand it. I don't understand everything, but, yes, I do understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, just -- you say there are translation issues in the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the English version, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the English version. Have they been raised before, have we missed anything? Because this is what is at this moment in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe it has been raised before and I don't recall focussing on this paragraph. Quite honestly, Mr. President, we -- I haven't gone through all the transcripts to check the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine that you didn't do that. Mr. Radic, since the Gotovina Defence would like to draw the attention of the Chamber to certain issues in relation to this document, this is preferably done in your absence. So, therefore, with my apologies, would you be kind enough to follow the Usher so that we can deal with that matter, and we -- I think that we'll see you back very soon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we don't have the English on the screen anymore. But I believe temporally it is mixed up, so what it should say is that: "Today Vojnic has 51 residents. It's a town of 15.000 people in which tomorrow we can put 15.000 people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say Vojnic has today only 51 inhabitants. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which -- any other matter? This, of course, extends, I take it, to the lines that follow, that we should understood the reference to 14 inhabitants of Lapac as of today -- today, at the 11th of August, 1995, and that -- yes, that seems to be ... Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- obviously I don't speak Croatian but I do know that these numbers correspond exactly to the numbers in the census. In other words, if you look at the 1991 census, the town of Vojnic had 51 Croats and Donji Lapac had 14. So in that sense it's more consistent with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- the translation as it is so perhaps we can get some [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then -- let's then --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- definitive clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can ask clarification from the witness. Mr. Misetic, what words exactly in your view are mistranslated and, as we all know, it's not the task of our interpreters to make corrections. At the same time, to send it back to CLSS for one or two words which are not perhaps very difficult issues and then to wait for a day might not be very practicable. Could you point us at where and perhaps reads it in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where it is said that it is today that Vojnic has 51 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I propose, Mr. President, that I just read out the -- from where it says: "I don't -- and I don't know ..." and I will just read the rest of it. And then ... It's in the second line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. I haven't got it in e-court in front of me. The page number in the hard copy would be ... yes, I see it. That's page 11 out of 18 in the hard copy. Yes, if you would please slowly read from, "I don't know," but then, of course, in the original language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "And I don't know, we don't have a report on this, but I don't know if you know that Vojnic has only 51 inhabitants today. It's a town of 15.000 people, and tomorrow we can fill it up with 15.000."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, logic does not oppose against this interpretation, because if today it is a town of 15.000 people, tomorrow we can fill it up with 15.000 doesn't make sense. Whereas, if you link today to the 51 inhabitants, it makes more sense. But we could verify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'm not opposed to the clarification. I just wanted to point that fact out. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll proceed, and we'll invite the witness to be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, an issue was raised in relation to the translation into English. I will read now in English what appears to be agreed upon by the parties at least, as a basis for proceeding. But I would, at the same time, like to very much invite you to carefully look in the text of what is now translated to you in B/C/S reflects what you understand is in the original minutes of the meeting. Then I start at the same point again: "That Vojnic has only 51 inhabitants today. It is a town of 15.000 people, tomorrow we can fill it up with 15.000, in addition, Lapac has 14 inhabitants. 14 Croats. Donji Lapac, 14 inhabitants. (It's more than the number of houses ...)." Are you --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is consistent now, both the English and the B/C/S versions are consistent with each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I continue my quote, because as -- where it says "It's more than the number of houses," then there are a few dots. I then continue: "I agree, but it's strategically so important, and it's in such a position that we must repair the houses, Gojko, and put Croats there, such is the position of the place." Could you briefly explain what you considered to be the strategic importance? If you could do it briefly. And I'm talking about Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about the time immediately in the aftermath of Operation Storm and the area where Croatia was practically cut off by the aggressor's army. There were only a few kilometres left -- of territory left between Karlovac and Kupa where one could travel from north to south. It is also a time when the war, in the immediate vicinity right across the border in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was still very intense and Mladic's forces were in a position where they were almost launching attacks and they certainly had opportunity to launch attacks again, to cut off Croatia one more time if this area was left vacant. So this was the strategic thinking that we were guided by. But I would like to add something. Not only during Operation Storm or around Operation Storm, but as early as the -- establishment of the Croatian state in 1990, we were considering and thinking about regions that were relatively empty, sparsely populated, because Croats had been actually expelled from there by the Communist parties in the past. So the strategic goal was that Croatian citizens not be for the most part in Zagreb, in other words, that Zagreb shouldn't be the -- in its number half of Croatia, but that Croatian citizens should also live in this area as well. So this was our thinking, that this was a region that needed to be settled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you now, the line, "It's more than the number of houses," and then the dots, do you remember what you exactly said at the time; and could you tell us what you then meant by what you said. We have only the line, "It's more than the number of houses."

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I think perhaps the transcript was imprecise. I had occasion to see some other transcripts and I know that they're not always absolutely reliable in terms of their precision. But I have to say that there were many apartments in this area, so not private homes but apartments, flats, and in almost 90 per cent of the cases, these flats, or apartments were actually socially owned or state owned. I don't even know how to interpret socially owned [B/C/S spoken] into English. But during the socialist period, all of us, and I'm referring to Yugoslavia, were actually just tenants using socially owned flats. So in Donji Lapac or Knin there were a lot of apartments that were actually owned by the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could be of some assistance on how these transcripts have been transcribed. And I'm not just looking at this one in isolation but through all of them. I don't know if -- if you want me to do this in the presence of the witness and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- focus on that which is in the parentheses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My first question for the witness was whether he has recollection of what he said and that is I -- I already indicated that the transcript may not be complete here. So I would first like to hear an answer to that question. If at any later stage we would like to focus more on how these transcripts were made, then we'll certainly do so and you can raise the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My first question was whether you remember about what you said about it's more -- apparently referring to the number of 14, because if you are talking about it's more than what is recorded here as the number of houses, that seems to relate to the number of 14. Do you remember what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. But I just realised now what's written here in the brackets, in the transcript, and I can only assume that perhaps this was an aside that somebody else actually said and that that's how it actually found its way into this transcript, because I don't see any logic in this, in a person who would be taking these minutes to put some words into parentheses in this way, and which makes this sentence incomplete, in fact. So I can't -- I absolutely cannot recall what it was that I was actually saying. I couldn't say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So whether you said it or someone else said it that's ... Now, could you explain to us what may have been meant by the speaker at the time, that 14 was more than the number of, as is said here, houses, which suggests that there was apparently, as far as houses are concerned, that there were less than 14.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I think this is just something that found its way into this transcript from elsewhere because I cannot place it in the context in which this is being said. So I have to be quite honest. I can't remember what my words were, but I couldn't even draw any conclusions as to what these words were actually referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Donji Lapac, was by majority, inhabited by persons of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: The large -- a large majority of the Donji Lapac population were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Large" could -- would that be 80 per cent, 90 per cent, 70 per cent? Do you have --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I think over 90 per cent, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- thank you. Could I take you briefly to P463. Page 12 in the English; pages -- page 17 in the B/C/S, at the bottom. This is a -- these are minutes of a meeting in which, on the cover page, as you may see on your screen now, it was you who was present, and as we understand, with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go to the pages I indicated. Could we go to the ... perhaps first -- no. First go to, in the original, page 17 in e-court, the last bottom. There -- but if you want to read it first, you talk about Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps we should move to the next page in B/C/S. There you are reported to have said: "Do you know that ethnically the cleanest municipality in Croatia was Donji Lapac, the cleanest." In view of your previous answer, could we understand that to be as the cleanest, in terms of the -- the highest majority being Serb?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said before, over 90 per cent. Here it says 99 per cent. But, yes, we can take it to mean that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the President said: "Probably none of them remained?" With a question mark. And you would have answered: "Yes, none."

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is the period after Storm, and in spite of the appeals by President Tudjman, the government, and all of us to stay, the population still left. I cannot specifically say whether nobody remained in Lapac, but a large majority did leave that area. This is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to move back to P462. That's the minutes of the meeting we just looked at. That's the minutes of the meeting of the 11th of August. We have looked already at the front page.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the bottom of page 14, we find that you are the person speaking. And once we've seen that, I'd like to move on to page 15. Could we move to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wanted to show in the English version that - it is on page 14 in English - that Mr. Radic is reported as being the speaker. And we then move to page 15 and page 23 in B/C/S. You're reported here as having said - and perhaps you could please try to find it - that: "The Law on Property authorises the state to grant that property for temporary use." Have you found that? I think it would be the [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I see it. It's at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Nikica Valentic is reported as having responded that: "This law regulates the possibility of granting that property and that somebody cannot be expelled from a house in a year time if" -- and then it says -- or at least we have it, between slashes: "/a refugee/ comes back. But the fact is," and I'm still quoting Mr. Valentic, "that we must think what we will be in two, three years, when somebody comes back." Then Mr. Susak stated that: "Nobody will move in under such law." To which Mr. Vrdoljak then responded: "Nobody will, but let's say, according to the Law on Compensation, this would definitely mean their final removal. Those from there would request to be sent few Kunas and would be very happy." Now, one possible interpretation of these remarks is that the Law on Property, the suggested Law on Property, would aim at guaranteeing persons who were granted property for temporary use, that they would not be expelled if the refugee who owned the house returned so that the refugees would not return, and I'm saying this is one of the possible interpretations. Is there any information available to you which would contradict such an interpretation of what is said here?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, some people thought in this way, and I agree with you that this is one possible way of thinking about it. Those of us who dealt with the renewal and the reconstruction thought differently, and we implemented this in the forthcoming period and there were many examples. For example, I think it's possible to show this even in video footage. In Kistanje we built an entire new settlement of 150 houses and relocated people to those houses who were temporarily accommodated in abandoned property, and then we freed up that property for the return of their owners once they decided to return. So we always took care of one type and the other type of person whenever this was possible, because the concept of the law was the preservation and guarantee of private property but also providing shelter to people who, at that time, were without homes, because they were, for example, expelled from Bosnia-Herzegovina or from other parts of Croatia. One more thing, which is perhaps the most important one here. The proper way to save a house from destruction was to have somebody inhabit it, either its real owner or a temporary tenant. As far as homes and especially estates in villages or forests were left empty, that house would be destroyed by thieves, robbers, by bad weather or other reasons. The goal was to preserve property at all costs and also to provide shelter for people and not to prevent anybody who wanted to return, who wanted to apply, who wanted to come back as a Croatian citizen could do that. This was something we didn't wish to prevent but it was a long process. It took a few months. However, if a house was left empty, it would become rundown and dilapidated within six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You started your answer by saying: "Yes, some people thought in this way ..." Did you refer to those speaking that they considered that this would finally result in a final removal, and is that also expressed by the speaker who says, Well, we can't expel them within a year; but what, if in two or three years somebody comes back, which is --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: It's hard to say what a person thought. But can I tell you what I personally thought at the time. I was personally in charge of creating such conditions. As for what individuals thought, well, it would be hard for me to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our primary focus at this moment is to understand what persons speaking in this meeting said. If you may have other thoughts, that seems to be already emerged from the first part of your answer where you said, Some people thought in that way. The thought as I put it to you, as a possible interpretation, that the -- that the -- the person speaking may have hinted at a non-return of refugees. Those who had left the area where they had lived. Was that on the mind of some persons, and could this be understood possibly as an expression of those thoughts, not to say that those were your thoughts. Perhaps we come back to that at a later stage. But I'm just focussing on this part of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I cannot say in any way what somebody else was thinking. If we read this record, these minutes, it's clear that there are individuals who could have said something like that, but these are not people who were charged with organising this particular task. Those whose message was crucial, important, that was the president of the republic, the prime minister, and then that was also me, it was my task. So I would not want to go into what that was supposed to mean, what was the message that person was trying to send when he said that at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to stay on the same page. The last part of what I just read to you was that Mr. Vrdoljak remarked that: "Those from there would request to be sent few Kunas and would be very happy." Now, these words could be interpreted as to suggest that compensation should be offered to displaced persons so that they would not return but accept a few Kunas. Is there any information you could provide to this Chamber which would contradict or shed a different light on what was said in this line by Mr. Vrdoljak?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. We began an assistance programme for expelled persons sometime in 1991 and 1992 in Croatia. These were Croats who had been expelled in Croatia. In the beginning, they were given money instead of having their homes reconstructed. They stayed in big towns. The funds they would receive for the reconstruction of their home in Nustar, which was partially liberated, but they never renovated the house. They would stay in Zagreb and use the money to buy a car, for example. So in principle, we abandoned the idea, and we put that into a law, of giving people money, but we actually did the renovations for their houses and in order to help them return to their homes, in order to prevent the money being spent for other purposes. So maybe Mr. Vrdoljak knew this fact and that there was such examples among the Croats, but this was not something that we strived for. We tried with the money that we had at our disposal to create conditions for these people to return where they came from. I mentioned the example of Kistanje where this was actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well, that the remark by Mr. Vrdoljak, "Those from there would request to be sent a few Kunas and would be very happy," that that would relate to Croats, or would it refer to Serbs who had left their homes?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: In this case, since this happened shortly after Oluja, I think he meant Serbs. But immediately before that, he did have some experience in relation to Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to move on to another document, Mr. Radic, to P2593. Perhaps we could look at the first page, to start with. Mr. Radic, you are reported to be present in the meeting, a meeting of the 17th of December, 1996. The same applies as earlier, may I take it that if you are mentioned at the cover page, that we could start on the basis of the assumption that you would be ready -- you would be present, and if there's anything at a later stage which would make you think that that might be a mistake, we'd like to hear from you. Could we then move to page 3, to start with, in the English, and page 4 in B/C/S. There, Mr. Ivica Kostovic is recorded as having said -- and perhaps we could move a little bit further down in the English. "The second thing that needs to be done -and the prime minister has already given the green light for it - is the simple compensation, meaning that we would pay off the Serbs, and" -- And we now move to page 4 in the English: "... our bank would give a loan to a Croat, he would give that money to a Serb, and the Serb would sign he would not return there anymore." And then on, I quote further from page 4 in the English, page 5 in the B/C/S, President Tudjman is recorded as having said: "They should be offered to be compensated for what they have here instead of return ..." These remarks could be interpreted to suggest that compensation should be offered to displaced persons so that they would not return. Could you tell us of any information which would -- which would you have and could tell the Chamber about which would contradict such an interpretation, that the focus was rather on compensation with the result that there would be no return? At least no return of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: There were different ideas voiced at our meetings. Obviously, I can't recall this, this was one of such ideas, but ultimately, this was not accepted as a conclusion and it was not acted upon. We set off the idea to consider buying out property from those who did not wish or were not going to come back a few years later. At that point in time, however, these ideas were not accepted as a conclusion, and I as the minister in charge and neither the prime minister nor the President issued any kind of instructions for this idea to be carried through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that you say, from what was said here, although not accepted, that the priority would be for compensation which would result in non-return but you say this was not put in practice later. I'm mainly focussing at this moment on how to interpret what was said and not to pay a lot of attention on what, after that happened, because the Chamber has heard quite some evidence on what was done at a later stage. I'm primarily focussing on the language used and the thoughts expressed at that time. Would you agree that this suggests, then, that compensation would be the first thing to do and then this would result likely in the no return? Apart from what happened later.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: At the time, I understood that slightly differently then, and today, still. Everything should be done for them to return, and as for those who decide not to return, a way had to be found to compensate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that if that was the guiding thought, that you would have expected language such as, Let's give them an option either to be compensated or to return, and if they choose not to return, then compensation is still there. That is what you would expect if the thoughts were as you just interpreted them.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: This was repeated at least 100 times at various meetings that I attended. This is one such meeting where this was said slightly differently. But it was stated in many meetings and publicly, as well as at government meetings, what you have just said, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you point us at any non-public government meeting where an offer for compensation was put on the same level as the option for return?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question. Compensation on the same level as the option for return?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, because we see here that they should be offered to be compensated instead of return. That seems to be an expression of a policy considered by the speaking person. Now, can you point us at any non-public meeting where you said it was phrased some times slightly different and it was expressed often in such meetings. Could you point us at any non-public government meeting or another non-public meeting, in which the option to be compensated and the option to return were offered, or were suggested to be offered as equal options, not the one that should be the aim of the policy to be adopted rather than the other, but you say if they would not return we could still compensate them. But could you point us at any non-public meeting where it was said, We should give them the free option: Return or be compensated, as you wish, and we'll opt for such an approach.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: At the time, we had cabinet meetings every morning at 9.00. And it's been 15 years since then, but it's my impression that practically each meeting did discuss return first. These ideas about compensation were in the background, because we simply didn't have the money. These were ideas of some people. I cannot remember, but I can see from the minutes that some people did voice these ideas. But that was not the most important thing. The key thing was to create conditions for all people to return, both Serbs and Croats, all those who wished to return, who wanted to take Croatian nationality. That was -- or citizenship. Croatian citizenship. That was the question. And immediately we opened at our branch -- our office in Belgrade - it still wasn't an embassy then, but it was an office - we opened up the possibility for people to apply to return. This couldn't happen immediately and we couldn't have them returning in a -- spontaneously. It had to be organised in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has received a considerable body of evidence on this issue. Therefore, I'm not encouraging you to further elaborate on that, and if any of the parties would want to re-visit this matter, they are, of course, free to do so. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know we're approaching a break and I so have an interpretation or translation issue and I didn't wish to interpret you in your questioning but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- perhaps we can ask the witness to leave when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would -- one final question. You said, Well, return was more important for us because we didn't even have the money to compensate them. Under those circumstances, I would expect President Tudjman to say, Let's do our best that they will return, because we have no money for compensation. Instead, he says, They should be offered to be compensated for what they have here instead of return, which gives a priority for compensation, at least that's how you could understand this, rather than a priority for return. Therefore, your explanation, We didn't have the money for compensation, earlier a few Kunas were mentioned, that -- I'm trying to reconcile your observation with what I read here as being said by President Tudjman and also the few Kunas, who talked about a few Kunas, I think it was Mr. Vrdoljak. I'm trying to reconcile your explanation, saying that, We didn't wish to compensate them, let them return, because we have no money.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: At the time, and after this meeting, I had scores of conversations with President Tudjman, and I convinced him that what I was suggesting was right, and ultimately he accepted that. So his final position was not what is stated here. Perhaps it was an idea at one point in time, but the final position was what I said: Let us first create conditions for people to return. We must understand that at the time we were in the process of discussing and figuring out what we wanted to do, and then the final position of the President was, Let us offer the option of return, and let us organise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at a point where we have a break, Mr. Radic. Mr. Misetic wanted to raise a translation issue. Therefore, we'll not bother you with that. Could you already follow Madam Usher, and we'd like to see you back in approximately 25 to 30 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have the original on my screen so I'm going try to follow it in the English, but to my mind, we need to check the translation of the first paragraph on the screen in the English, the President's comment, and then Mr. Kostovic's follow-up which may affect what is actually being discussed there. I don't know if you wish me to read it out or just tell what you I think it should say. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would rather wait until you have verified the translation and then hear from you. Of course, still in the absence of the witness because you said, I still have to verify that, and that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, but I mean verify with the interpreters or if you wish to just tell me -- for me to tell you what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if would you read the relevant portion, and again I apologise for the interpreters, but for very practical reasons, if it doesn't become too complex because complex issues should be sent to CLSS for proper verification. But if there's an issue which you consider we could deal with and where I am not faced with any fierce objections by the interpreters, then you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- please introduce the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I also thank the interpreters. It's just that if we're -- we seem to be doing somewhat of an exegesis on these transcripts so I wanted to make sure that we have it perfectly correct. The sentence, Mr. Kostovic in the first paragraph starts and I will speak in Croatian now: "[Interpretation] The majority of them says, I will come back if you guarantee my safety. Naturally this is what they say but when they need to come, we have been waiting for 100 Serbs for a month, from Bilje, who want to come back but we still don't have that definite list." [In English] And then the President says: "[Interpretation] And they should be offered, instead of returning, to have compensation for this here and then" [In English] And then [Interpretation] "Or if they wish, Mr. President, Radic's men can find him some intact Serbian house and tell him, Here you are, here's a house, come back. The majority of them will not." [In English] Just in terms of the subtlety of the language here, Mr. President, the -- the change from census to a list, it seems to me that he is discussing 100 Serbs who were supposed to come back but they haven't got a list of who these Serbs are, and they have been waiting since August. The President says in Croatian [Interpretation] "And offer to them," [In English] meaning a reference, I believe, back to the 100 Serbs. And then in the next sentence, Mr. Kostovic says: We could offer them or Radic's men can offer them an entire or an undamaged Serb house. And it's been interpreted as, "They won't come back" which is accurate but I think there is a little more subtlety in it which is they don't want to come back [B/C/S spoken] meaning a personal decision as opposed to some other factors, et cetera. So I just -- the context of the questioning of the witness seemed to say that this was a broader conversation and I read it as they're discussing this return of the 100 Serbs from Bilje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time the witness testified that he had to convince President Tudjman that he was right, which I understood to be opposite to what President Tudjman expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as I understand the transcript, it is that he's being -- the president is being told that there are these Serbs who say they want to come back but we have been waiting for four months for them to do so and can't get a list yet of who they are. And then the president says, Well, to those, offer them something, and then there's a further response. That's just so that we're clear on what I think it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's put on the record. If this needs a new translation to be uploaded -- I do not know exactly. You have explained to us now how you understand this in the original language and we will certainly consider that. I was about to move to my next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I just wanted to make one additional point, and Mr. Kehoe had indicated it earlier. It is our understanding from doing many exegeses on these Presidential transcripts that when -- when -- and we can confirm that with the Prosecution during the break. When something is in parentheses when a speaker's portion, it usually means there is another voice that's heard on the tape, not the voice of the person speaking. So that's -- we just wanted to clarify when we were talking to Mr. Radic about on the 11th of August transcript, usually what that will mean is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I left it open that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- someone else was speaking when I then put my further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have a break, and we resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'd like to stay in the same document, P2593, but now move to page 14 in English and page 19 in B/C/S. And I would like to draw your attention to where it starts, I think in B/C/S, "trece," "third" in English. You are reported to have said there the following: "The Serbs are the most corrupt people in the world. There is isn't a single more corrupt or purchasable nation. Starting from this fact, I believe that we can achieve more, as we just said, by buying their property." Earlier you explained how some people were -- may have been thinking about giving priority to compensation but that that was not your view. This remark could be interpreted to suggest, and that's -- the question in that respect is similar to my previous questions, that compensation should be offered to displaced persons so that they would not return. Same question to you: What information could you provide to this Chamber which would contradict this possible interpretation of those words?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, just this, that this was one of the ways to do it, that this was one of the elements in the discussion, and as the discussion went on from day to day, we increasingly were reaching the conclusion that it was the correct thing to do, to offer everyone to return. And this transcript and many other transcripts from that time are just part of those discussions, and no final conclusions were actually put forth there. Me, myself, I wasn't quite clear at the outset what the best way to proceed would be, but after all these discussions and conversations and argumentation, discussions with my colleague Serbs also who were in Zagreb, we managed to reach the final position, which was that they should return. And this, although, as I mentioned earlier, there was the fact that we were aware there were not enough funds to actually cover the compensation plan at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, in December 1996 - that is, approximately 15 to 16 months after Operation Storm - your language does not suggest that you have no money. To the contrary, the language suggests that you can achieve much more by buying their property.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, this was the fact for those who had actually decided not to return. We have the following fact. We had already actually had a good picture of who was willing and going to return. Let me just remind you that we actually extended the time-line for applications for return by three months several times over. And after this, even those who directly took part in the rebellion in Croatia and who had not opted for Croatia as the state where they would finally wish to settle down, of course, for those individuals the final variant that would be offered, the final option would be to offer them money as compensation. But that was -- there were various options that were being discussed. And at this time, there was a third option which was actually sort of going on the sidelines which was exchange of property. There were a lot of people, Serbs from Croatia, even Serbs from large cities, from Zagreb, Zadar, and so forth, who actually exchanged their property with Croats who were actually people who had lived in Vojvodina and were born there, natives of Vojvodina. And there weren't -- this was not a small figure we're talking about. There were tens of thousands of people entering this kind of process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, not another translation issue, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm only doing translation issues, Mr. President. So it's just a -- actually it's interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you please point at the lines you consider not to be accurately translated so that we could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 36 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- line 10 in my e-court - let me just make sure -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it about at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what words then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, it is page 36, line 9, on the central LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 9, central LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The -- "on the sidelines."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I will read to you a sentence where there possibly is a problem with the translation. I read it to you, and after you have listened, once it is translated to you again, please tell us whether it reflects what you said. I start at the end of line 8, Mr. Misetic: "But that was -- there were various options that were being discussed. And at this time, there was a third option, which was actually going on the sidelines, which was exchange of property." What is now translated back to you, is there any inaccuracy compared to what you said?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I didn't say in parallel, running in parallel. But in fact it was the -- the essence is there. So there was a third option at the same time and it was going on without our knowledge. That was the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the sidelines, then, I take it, that was a discussion, which meant beyond your discussions.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was something that we didn't know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You considered, apparently, buying the property as a better achievement. The discussion as we have followed it from these texts is, Return or money to be paid, whether we call it compensation or buying property, that that is -- may come down to approximately the same. You said buying the property was the better achievement. Could you explain, in view of your other answers, why you considered where you were -- as you said, you were in favour of first offering return, while you, nevertheless, considered buying the property a better achievement?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, the basic principle -- our basic position was there aren't enough people in Croatia. Croatia had a major demographics problem and we wanted as large a number of people to return as possible. Those who wanted to be Croatian citizens. But as time went by, after two or three year, we realised that this was not an option, that there was a number of people who had left Croatia who didn't want that. So then the other option actually prevailed, that we should also find this other option which was the -- the sanctity of private property should be upheld and it should not be violated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do I understand that in your answer, where you said that, "We had a major demographic and we wanted as large a number of people to return as possible," that that would include Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: No dilemma at all, both Croats and Serbs, because large swaths of Croatian territory were sparsely populated, or unpopulated, even before Storm, and this was even more true after the war, or in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are here in late 1996. I'm not aware of -- let's say, a general call, Croats and Serbs, say, Please all come back, Croats and Serbs, and populate the areas which are so badly populated, almost empty of inhabitants. Could you point at any -- well, let's say in this period of time, that is August of 1995 to December 1996, where there was such a -- kind of a general call, We need people to inhabit our country. Whether you are of Serb ethnicity or of Croat ethnicity, please come back and be in our population.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, not only that this was a general invitation, it was much more than that. But I'm not certain whether this was in 1996 or 1997, but I personally proposed a law on areas of special state interest, and for the most part, they covered the areas in question, where we not only invited people to come back but we actually stimulated this by -- by providing tax incentives, large or higher salaries to those professions that were wanted. So if a doctor, for instance -- and nobody spoke -- nobody mentioned Serbs or Croats. Doctors, if they wanted to come and live in Donji Lapac, or any of the areas that we had proclaimed as areas of special state interest, they would actually receive higher pay than a doctor in Zagreb. So it was much more than a general invitation. There was a law that was passed in the Assembly and, of course, this was an additional expense, but we couldn't actually provide sufficient incentive for people to come back and settle down in those areas without this kind of stimulus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say that they were better paid than a doctor in Zagreb, that suggests that you would primarily address Croats because there were no many Serb doctors in Zagreb, were they?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: No. We were actually addressing our invitation to Croatian citizens, absolutely to everyone who wanted to proceed in that way. This was a law that was passed. You can take a look at the law, and there is not a single article in it which would actually identify people according to their ethnic background. Simply this was a attempt to revitalise these regions. And if I may just add, at about the same time - I can't tell you the exact date - but again at my initiative, the Assembly actually adopted a national programme for demographic renewal. And again, there's not a single article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll come -- I'll come to that later. My next question does focus, however, on legislation to be adopted. And I'd like to move back to P462. That's the same 11th of August meeting we looked at before, Mr. Radic. Page 15 in English; page 24 in B/C/S. Yes. I'd like to draw your attention what was said by Mr. Krpina, and I quote from what he is recorded to have said. He says: "... I think we should pass a law, they would declare all abandoned property state property on the pretext of preserving it [sic] and then in the procedure, if someone returns, if there are no legal obstacles, the state will give him back his property." This remark suggests, or at least could be interpreted, that the preservation of property, in the mind of Mr. Krpina, was used as a pretext for declaring abandoned property state property but that preservation was not the law's actually purpose [sic]. Could you -- same question. Do you have any information which would go against such an interpretation of his words?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I do, in the events themselves, which followed, which was that this property was actually preserved and returned. And, again, I have to repeat, there were numerous discussions and various proposals put forward and there were many situations where a proposal -- where a conclusion -- or, rather, a meeting ended with a majority thinking one thing, a majority of the participants, and then later on, after a discussion with the prime minister and President Tudjman, we actually reached conclusions that were non-discriminatory by nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, this Chamber has heard evidence from a witness, Mr. Galbraith, who was, at the time, the US ambassador to Croatia. And he testified - and for the parties I'm referring to transcript page 5.203 - with regard to passing a law declaring abandoned property state property, he stated that: "The notion of preserving the property was simply a pretext for taking the property, making it impossible for the Serbs who had left to return to that property, and as part of a scheme to try to resettle Croats in the area, thereby changing its strategic -- the strategic complexion of the Krajina from being Serb to being Croat." Now, Mr. Galbraith used very similar words as the words we just read as being used by Mr. Krpina on the 11th of August. Again, would you have any specific information which would contradict what Mr. Galbraith told us, how he perceived the intentions, and that could undermine his testimony that preservation was used as a pretext for declaring abandoned property state property so that Serbs would not return. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, Mr. President, I believe that Mr. Galbraith was referring to this transcript if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check that, T52 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I know that during the course of his direct examination he was shown this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The reason I recognise that is because I objected to it, but be that as it may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say that the similarity of the language not very striking --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you put it to him. Nevertheless his testimony is such that he would not say, Well, I never thought about that being the intention behind it. I mean, if you wish, we could -- or in cross-examination could go through his testimony. But I do agree with you, I -- I should verify. But I take it that he was shown the -- he was shown the -- the document, the -- the minutes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least -- yes. Yes, but, of course, then still what remains is his testimony. I might go into that into further detail but I would have to properly prepare that and find the right portions of his testimony and every detail in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Right. With regard to that document, just one last point. I do believe we will find that it was admitted through Mr. Galbraith, P462.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it may well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, leave alone that perhaps the language pretext was -- was perhaps suggested to him by looking at the document. I would like to take you, then, briefly to your statement given to the Gotovina Defence, and if you would allow, just read a portion of that at this moment and if there is any further need to contextualise I will hear from you. In paragraph 33 of the statement, as it was presented to the Chamber, it says that you stated that: "Some of the representatives of the international community exerted pressure on the Republic of Croatia with respect to return, but they did not understand, or didn't want to understand, the true reality of the situation in the field." Which suggests that pleading for the return was something you could only do on not a proper understanding of the reality. Could you, first of all, confirm that this is what you said, as we find it in the statement; and, then, second, comment on that?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can confirm this by saying the following. Some representatives of the international community, including Mr. Galbraith, exerted pressure on Croatia for the return to be allowed immediately before the conditions were ready, before the infrastructure was renewed, before the area was actually organised in a way to allow -- to provide for normal living conditions. So that what is I had in mind. We did not have in mind a long period of time but, rather, a short transitional period. And if you allow me, just one additional sentence about what Ambassador Galbraith said. The fact -- I mean, the proof that he was not correct in what he thought is that his successor, Mr. Montgomery, found a way for the American government to assist our programme of building homes in Kistanje, where he and I together actually gave the keys over to the new owners to -- and where we actually made sure that Serbs moved into those homes. So our intention was not to prevent it but, rather, to allow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, at least part of the answer was that Mr. Galbraith said that what he read was completely consistent with what he observed. So as to make clear that even if the wording may have been borrowed, that the testimony does take distance from -- from what he read in this minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And my -- my thought, Mr. President, was simply the -- the similarity of wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then I would like to stay in P462; page 16 in the English, and 25 in B/C/S. Mr. Valentic is recorded as having said -- no, let me first go to what President Tudjman is recorded of having said. And I don't see that on my screen at this moment. Yes, it's on the bottom of the page. President Tudjman is there recorded as having stated: "I am with the more radical. If someone has left the country and does not appear there, I don't know, a month, or three months, et cetera, that shall be considered, think of the wording, state property, et cetera. We have come out of a war, et cetera, define it like that." Which -- and perhaps I -- we move on to page 17 in the English, 26 in B/C/S, where Mr. Valentic is speaking. He is recorded to have stated: "Not three months, three months is too long, because we ..." And then President Tudjman says: "Okay, a month, then." This language could be interpreted as expressing the thought that the deadline for declaring abandoned property as state property should be kept very short. Do you have any explanation as to why President Tudjman and why Mr. Valentic were -- were wanting this to be such a short period?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I think what is key here is this. In those areas where there were no problems that I mentioned earlier, such as the removal of land-mines and so on, that people should return as soon as possible so that the property would not get damaged. But when we saw that the deadlines that we provided did not really produce any results, then we extended the deadlines in many instances. There were a lot of apartments, flats, in small towns, for instance, I was in Benkovac and then in Knin, where if a person returned very soon, it was still possible to salvage that apartment. When I said earlier that conditions were not such to allow for people to move that, because the land-mines hadn't been removed and so on, but there were cases where we -- the conditions were such that people could return very soon. And this should not be understood in a negative sense. Rather, it should be understood as an incentive. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If my recollection serves me well, this Chamber has not received evidence in which it was explained that the longer period of time for return was inspired by the fact that it was not safe due to land-mines to return any earlier. The Chamber did receive some evidence quoting different reasons and -- but the parties will correct me when my recollection is not correct. Some of the evidence said that there was a lot of international pressure on it, and not land-mines. But if the parties could assist me in finding any piece of evidence where the land-mines are used as an explanation for why the 30 days should be longer, then I would -- the Chamber would appreciate it. But first the question: Do you have -- the land-mines, which you give now as an explanation, is there any -- is there any documentary evidence or is there any other information you could provide to the Chamber that this is what caused the change of the time-limits? And the Chamber is aware of how the time-limits changed; that is, late August, a decree, 30 days; then 22nd of September, from 30 to 90 days; and then, finally, in January 1996, the time-limit being abolished at all. So the Chamber is aware of these, I would say, legislative developments, but since the fact that it was not safe to return because of mine clearance is, as far as I -- as far as my recollection goes, is new. Do you have any corroboration for that view as having triggered the extension of time?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I'm going back to that period in my thoughts. The overall return was under my charge, both of Croats and Serbs. There was a danger that Croats who had spent three or four years in exile, for example, from the place of Slunj, would not suddenly rush back within a day or two, without us having checked the -- whether the houses were de-mined or not. So when I'm talking about the return to the area liberated during Oluja, I'm talking about the return of all persons, regardless of their names. So the first major problem was the problem of mines and de-mining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether there -- you have any documentary evidence to corroborate this explanation of extending the 30 days' time-limit. Any minutes, any documents, any decrees.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I haven't really been dealing with that subject for -- topic for ten years. I'm not in the state government anymore. So my recollection is what it is. What I seem to remember is that we had that deadline for a certain reason and also because an insufficient number of people had applied to return within that 30-day period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No international pressure on extending the time-limits, as far as your recollection goes?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think that there were talks with certain ambassadors who did provide some suggestions in that direction, yes. But my recollection is more of this later period, when we extended it for a year or longer, when we were preparing a conference, a donors' conference and equipment, where the international community was supposed to help in the rebuilding, overall building. So that's when we had conversations and deadlines and pressure to extend the deadlines for the return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of specific instances where you provided, if I could say, the same de-mining services to Serbs who wanted individually to go back to the place where they had lived before? Because you said that's what you did with Croats returning. Do you have any recollection of giving the same de-mining services to -- to Serbs? Any specific instances or ...

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: De-mining was never aimed at a particular house but it was aimed at a certain region, an area. When a certain area was being de-mined, then all the citizens from the -- that particular area would have the same service. And I must say, on the topic of de-mining, that we had a lot of help from the international community. If ever any help came in that particular job, it came from the international community, and because they were the ones who were providing this assistance, it would never be something that was aimed at only one ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on the issue of de-mining, I don't believe this transcript is in evidence as 65 ter 939. December 4, 1995. I was just directed to it by my learned friend Mr. Kay where General Cervenko is talking about the difficulties in returns because of those de-mining -- because of the mine problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There is a considerable amount in this transcript, Your Honour. It is a 61-page transcript. There is mention of the United Nations. It was a document I was aware of when Your Honour raised that -- that matter, so I turned it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is appreciated. I invited you even to -- to -- I said as far as my recollection goes, I've not seen anything in evidence, which luckily is then confirmed by Mr. Kehoe that I didn't miss a major portion of the evidence. If could you provide a copy to Chamber's staff and, of course, usually we're not seeking evidence on our own initiative but since it was raised in this question, if we could have a look at it so as to see whether this would -- although the witness didn't give that information but to see whether it -- not now immediately. If would you take your time and provide it to Chamber's staff, then we may have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Apparently there is no English translation in e-court and quite how have I ended up with an English translation which isn't from my staff at all, I don't know. Mine's got "OTP" on the bottom left-hand corner so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that the parties sit together during the next break and see in what way they can provide the Chamber with any information and especially, also, on -- and that's, of course, the focus of my question in view of the answer of the witness, is Croats returning, we had to de-mine, and the question was, were similar services provided to Serbs returning. That was my -- because what we are talking about, we're talking about time-limits imposed on the return of those who had left the territory. So the Chamber might not be interested in the whole subject of de-mining as a general subject but specifically in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I suggest Your Honour reads this document, if Your Honour is interested in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certainly interested in it. I take it that you would then provide the other parties so that everyone knows what I'm reading, and I want to be very transparent in this respect. Ms. Gustafson, you have 61 pages to read overnight as well, as far as I understand. I'd like to move on and move to another meeting, which is, again, a Presidential meeting, 22nd of August; P463. And ... We have that on our screen. Mr. Radic, you are reported to be present here. I think we had a look at it already. I'd like to move to page 6 in English and page 9, to start with, in B/C/S and then move on to page 10. According to the record, President Tudjman stated that upon learning that the mayor of Knin was a Serb and was no good for anything, that the mayor should be replaced. And he added to that: "There is no reason for a Serb being there right now." And then you are recorded as having responded to that: "Sure. He shouldn't be there." And then President Tudjman then stated: "There's a majority of Croats there, so change that." Could you shed some light on President Tudjman, in August 1995, appearing to take the view that Knin should not have a Serb mayor?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: The emphasis is not on whether somebody is a Serb or a Croat, from what I can remember, but whether they are capable of being -- managing a town after Oluja, a town which is more complex than Zagreb. If I remember, I spoke about a number of mayors of towns where displaced persons were coming back, so I was thinking both of Croats and Serbs. Not only Serbs but also Croats which do not have enough self-initiative or are not good organisers or did not prove to be people up to the significant and difficult demands a town would require. And the President added to that the story about how in some area before the war or perhaps at that particular moment, there was one majority ethnic group or another, and he was thinking even of appointing somebody who would be accepted by the people who were there at that time, which is something that can then be reviewed after a certain period of time has passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what -- you introduce the mayor, and you say that he wasn't good for anything and that it was a Serb. Now, if it was not about his Serb ethnicity, I would have expected President Tudjman to say, There's no place for incompetent people. However, he says there is no reason for a Serb being there right now. He does not respond in any way to your observation as to be good for nothing, apart from what that exactly means, being good for nothing.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: The transcript goes on. Actually it's the only transcript that I read before I came here.
