You will see at the very end that we are also discussing the mayors in Istria, for example, or Dubrovnik, where I am warning the President that everything should be done for us to secure people of good quality in Croatian areas as well, particularly in places where the situation was problematic. This would be something that is very important for the return of displaced persons. I'm trying to recall the entire conversation not just a detail because the transcript is a transcript of an informal chat, in armchairs. It is not an official meeting, and we did not really state precise definitions or state our positions precisely. My position at the time was to warn the President, Let's go to some key towns and bring capable, able people to positions there, in those towns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the President responds by saying: "There's a majority of Croat there, so change that." Could you explain "the majority of Croats" at that point in time, and we're talking 22nd of August, being a majority in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: When we're speaking about Knin, we're talking about the broader area of the town. Knin also includes the nearby villages around the town, where, at that time, a number of Croats were able to return. Also, a large number of apartments was preserved in the town, where a number of people moved in that were needed for the normal functioning of the town. At that point, from what I remember, the majority of those people were Croats, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they had already moved in on the 22nd of August?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Not all. It was more about some of them could. I remember that we had a nearby village which was quite large, the village of Kijevo. So we had about 2.000 displaced persons in Split. The idea was that they could come to a state-owned property, apartments in Knin. I think this is stated in one of the transcripts. So they could at a distance of ten kilometres away from their homes physically help with the rebuilding of those houses and then move back into them. So logically, we needed somebody to come back with them who would be able to lead those people and manage the affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your explanation suggests that there was no majority of Croats there but that you envisaged that in the future there might be a majority of Croats. But that's not what President Tudjman says, is it?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I don't recall how many people there were at one particular point in time or at what date. I can't really remember that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that if all the Serbs would return, that Knin would be a Serb-majority town and that the same would be true for the Knin municipality as well?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. But we were aware of the fact that this was not possible at all, because a good number - I'm not going to say the majority - but a good number of the citizens of Knin were, let's say, officers of the Yugoslav People's Army who were attacking -- Croatia. They were not even people who originated from Knin. They just got apartments there. So they left. They still haven't accepted Croatia as their own state. We are aware of that. Knin, absolutely. Small towns such as Knin, Benkovac, they just didn't have the local population, people who actually came from there but a lot of people, especially those who were in the army, were settled there deliberately. So these towns did not only have native inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that a certain portion of the witness's answer concerning what features were in the town wasn't interpreted and may be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, where should I ask the witness, starting on what line, to repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 53, beginning at line 11: "They just got apartments there," and then there was something -- specific reason that he offered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read again part of your answer as it was translated to us and I invite you to complete it. You said: "But a good number of the citizens of Knin were, let's say, officers of the Yugoslav People's Army who were attacking -- Croatia." Was there anything you added there to your answer? Was there -- is there anything missing -- or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. There seems to be a problem with LiveNote being one line off depending on whether we're at our stations or the central LiveNote. So it was the next line down, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now it has moved from my screen so I have to get the other version. So you want me to start reading just prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, just after that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just after that. Okay. Therefore I again read to you what was translated to us: "... let's say, officers of the Yugoslav People's Army who were attacking -- Croatia. They were not even people who originated from Knin. They just got apartments there. So they left." What is missing in what I just read to you and was part of your answer?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: These were not natives of Knin had who had spent ten or 15 years living there and who had Croatian nationality, who would live there and consider themselves citizens of Knin. They were on temporary work in Knin. We would -- we could look at them like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you referring to people who had moved in since the -- since Croatia lost control over their territory, so since 1991? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Partly about them, and partly those who, as officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, were given apartments in Knin, spent some time there, then they would move to Nis. Then from Nis they would relocate somewhere else. The emphasis was this. Those people when they left, of course, they didn't even think about going back to Croatia because Croatia was not their home. They were living there temporarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to understand what you meant exactly by "temporarily." Was that people that moved in since power was taken over; or are you also referring to an earlier period in time?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us what approximately was then the percentage of such imported inhabitants of Knin town and municipality, well, let's say, before the republic of --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I don't have that data but it was not an insignificant number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is it 10 per cent, 20 per cent? What's your understanding of what part of the population -- and I'm talking about pre-war, so before the Serb forces took control of the area of the -- as they called it, the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Precisely, preparations to take over control lasted for several scores of years. I cannot give you a specific number. But at least 30 per cent of people like that were located to Knin on duty, serving in the Yugoslav People's Army. That was the largest percentage of people who had relocated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if we would take the census of 1991, and if we would deduct 30 per cent of those having reported as Serbs in Knin town and Knin municipality, would we then approximately have some insight as to what was the Serb population of that area, not influenced by an influx of JNA officers perhaps for preparing the takeover? Would that be a fair way to look at it? Because then we might have a look at the census and then we could establish whether, if we're talking about a Croat majority or a Serb majority, what would have been the balance, excluding those who came in after 1991, excluding those who were there stationed as JNA officers, so that we get to what I would suggest to call the core of the Serb population of Knin municipality and Knin town. I don't have the figures at hand. We would have to look at it. But I'm just seeking your position in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I don't have them either. This would require a more serious demographic analysis. But we're probably close to these figures, if we're talking about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now going back to the transcript of that meeting, when President Tudjman said something about the majority of Croats there and said, "So change that," you then are recorded as having stated: "Yes, sure. They wanted to put some Serb in Okucani as well. Not a chance. A Croat is over there and we did Okucani nicely." I notice reading this, that you did not refer to an incompetent Serb, which, whoever would wish to be put in Okucani, but about they wanted to put some Serb, only reference to ethnicity, nothing else, and then you said, "Not a chance." Could you first tell us, Okucani, was the composition -- the ethnic composition of Okucani was approximately what? We can verify it if you would like to, but not the whole of the census of 1991, and I'm now looking at the old figures is in evidence yet. What was Okucani composed of ethnically.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I think that they were in the majority before the war, but now we're talking about the situation when these socially owned or state apartments were occupied by Croats who were left homeless in Posavina, across the area, and there was some ideas to leave the mayor who was in office before, not that he was in Okucani from before but he was a mayor while in exile. And what they proposed was a man who had been leading them, a man whom they trusted. But I never personally discriminated or distinguished between people as Serbs and Croats but as people who would be able to manage or be part of a group. When taken out of context it could be interpreted that we were picking mayors based on whether they were Serbs or Croats, but, no, that was really not the goal at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said: "They were in the majority before the war." You were referring to Serbs? Or Croats?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbs were in the majority. The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as to that majority being 55 per cent, or 75, or 95? Was that a large majority?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I think the ratio was not so pronounced. The figures were quite similar in those areas, but please don't hold me to the figures. I really don't have the data in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think from the pre-war period, the 1991 census at least, the parties could assist the Chamber in having more accurate figures on that. I put this question to you because the reference you make in this meeting is to ethnicity, and, therefore, if you say it should be looked into in the context, that's exactly why we are asking you questions, so that you also have an opportunity to give us the context and give us a better understanding of -- a better possibility of understanding of what was said and what was meant.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in this unrelated conversation that we had, and that's what this conversation of the 22nd of August was, where we discussed all kinds of topics, we did not insist on people actually expressing their views. I frequently used the term "Croat" when I refer - and that is the case today as well - to Croatian citizens. And at that time, well, in my office, as a university professor, I had four assistant lecturers, two of whom were ethnic Serbs. In other words, I don't have any kind of bias -- negative bias towards them. When I say "Croat," I mean a Croatian citizen, a person who has in mind the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we move to our next subject, I would like to have a break first, because we will not finish that in two or three minutes. We have a break until ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we proceed, I'd like to address one matter very briefly. Earlier today we discussed, and I'll not go into any details, about something being filed by Friday, and the other parties still considered whether or not -- you remember what it was. We dealt with the matter in private session. Now the Chamber would like, even if the filing would come on Friday at the end of the day, already be informed by noon whether or not any choice has been made, because if the Chamber would consider to take further action, we'd rather do that Friday afternoon, in order not to lose further time. So I said please file it by Friday but already inform Chamber's staff by noon what they can expect more specifically also in relation to names.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we continue, Mr. Radic -- Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just on this because whatever application is made by one party, the other parties will -- may want to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm concerned that the Court may implying that decisions are being made before responses to filings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, if no one applies for A, B, or C --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then the Chamber feels free to do what it may have already on its mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be any submission which leaves it open that the Chamber should continue to show self-restraint, we'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is no reason for self-restraint, and that is when none of the parties have indicated to take any action in relation to A, B, or C, then the Chamber feels more free in proceeding in -- as it intended, in relation to A, B, and C. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that meet your concern, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. If there are amendments to be made, I do alert the Court to issues that might be arising which will involve discovery issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine that. We have to carefully consider how we can proceed without obstructing -- for the Chamber not to obstruct parties initiatives and that's on our mind, and we will certainly find ways to do that. At the same time, the Chamber, by being properly informed even about some details, will better be able to assess whether it can send an e-mail, make a phone call, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour more clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And close communication here can avoid any risk of unrepairable damage. Then I would like to move on. Mr. Radic, sometimes we have to deal with urgent procedural matters. We are in 463, and I'd like to move to page 10 in the English and page 14 and 15 in the B/C/S. And I read again what -- and perhaps we should -- no, perhaps we should go back to -- where are we? Are we in 14 in the B/C/S. One second, please. Yes. I -- I again read to you what the portion of the minutes is, which I would like to ask you some questions about. You said -- oh, no, it -- you're recorded to have said: "I defined five priorities according to the urgency of colonising these places with Croats. "If you ask me, this thing right here is the first and second priority. We should bring Croats back here urgently and this area should be urgently colonised with Croats. And we should by no means let more than 10 per cent of Serbs be here ever again. Because, that's where we were cut off." Where President Tudjman then responds: "Not even 10 per cent." First of all, talking about "here," and -- what area did you have on your mind when you made this statement?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I was showing a map to President Tudjman, and I was referring to the area between the rivers Kupa and Una. That's the area where the Croatian territory is the narrowest, where it had almost been cut in two. For instance, sometime between Karlovac -- somewhere between Karlovac and all the way to Ogulin, this was a strategically important area. I have already mentioned it earlier today. And here we were still discussing these matters because there was still the threat of Mladic's army's aggression from Bosnia because it very active there at the time. So I was pointing to the President the area between the rivers Kupa and Una.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you translate that for the Chamber in municipalities. What municipalities would be covered by what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, these were -- at the time those municipalities were larger than they are today. But certainly the town of -- the city of Karlovac with its surrounding areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. If you say the municipalities are larger now, I do not mind if you would refer to municipalities as they were in, well, let's say, 1991. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. At one time Croatia had some 50 municipalities, whereas today it has some 500, and that is why it is difficult to point this out without a map, actually. That's why I mentioned the area between the rivers Una and Kupa, where the state was -- almost cut in half. But if you had the map before you, that would be the area between Slunj and Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could check the witness's answer there, what the area is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you repeat what the area was because there may be a -- I didn't look at the transcript, as a matter of fact, but could you please repeat how you described the area. It is translated to us as the area between the rivers Kupa -- Kupa and Una, or is it at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He mentioned some cities, Mr. President, at the end of the sentence. If could just name the cities again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that the reference on page 62, somewhere around line 18, Slunj, Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said: "... if had you the map before you, that would be the area between Slunj and --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: The towns of Karlovac, Slunj and to the south all the way to Ogulin. That's the area where Croatia is the thinnest, the territory is the narrowest, and during the occupation that's where it was at the greatest -- in the greatest danger. That is the area I was referring to and that's the area we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could be of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- some assistance in this regard. As you recall, there has been some marking of maps on this score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Granic has marked that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. And we have that map but we also have the blank of that. So as -- if Your Honour just wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that might be a good idea, that I -- but I do not what the blank map is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. What was admitted into evidence was the map that's marked. The blank map is 65 ter 1D3011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have that on our screen and could Madam Usher then assist so that we -- that it can be marked. We will get the map on our screen, Mr. Radic, so that we ...

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Maps usually take some time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could it be enlarged and can we focus on the -- we do not necessarily mean the whole of the map but that area to be ... Perhaps move the map a bit to the right. No, not the bar but the map. Yes. Madam Usher, could you assist the witness in marking the area he was referring to. Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it all and I can mention the municipalities now if you would like me to, because now can I see them before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do both. Let's invite you to mark the map and then also to name the municipalities which were covered by your observation.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: So I am talking about this area, this encircled area where the municipalities of Vrginmost, Vojnic, Karlovac, Duga Resa, and perhaps a portion of the Ogulin municipality, maybe even the larger part of Ogulin municipality, and the municipality of Slunj. So this was the an area that was of critical significance and in a critical -- at a critical point strategically speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you said that's where we were -- no, let's first ask you another question. You said: "We should by no means let more than 10 per cent of Serbs be here ever again." Do I understand that Serbs that would have left, that it was on your mind that if Serbs were to return, that the final result would be that there would never be more than 10 per cent after the return?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: No. I certainly did not say that anywhere. We were discussing the resettlement of Croats into that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whoever you want to settle there, the language used is: "By no means let no more than 10 per cent of Serbs be here ever again." Which suggests that, as the final result, that there would be no more than 10 per cent Serbs. I mean, whether you would fill the area with Croats or Italians or Germans is another matter. But this language, especially also if we look at the response by President Tudjman, could well be interpreted as saying, Whatever the return programme will be, finally, never more than 10 per cent Serbs there. That's, I would say, the -- unless you disagree with me, but this is what is my understanding of the ordinary language. If I say, Let there never be more than 10 Canadians winning gold medal, then it means not 11, not 12, not 13, not 14. 10 or less.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: But that would mean that 90 Croats might win the gold medal, if we are discussing gold medals. So what we are talking about here is a relatively empty area which is sparsely populated, not enough people live there, and if we were talking about the area before Operation Storm and talking about Operation Storm in talking about immigration into Croatia, we were of the view that they should not be actually -- they should not migrate to Zagreb but rather to these unsettled areas. Because we were first to develop the economy, to develop factories and various plants and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, a population will be 100 per cent. That's those who are living there. If you say, not more than 10 per cent should be Serbs, apart from who will be the remaining 90 per cent, what the Chamber is interested in to understand how many Serbs had been living there and which would be above the 10 per cent that was mentioned here. Could you tell us -- let's take an example. Vojnic, how many Serbs were there pre-war?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know off the top of my head what the figure would be, but we can add them up. If we take this whole area, this whole circle that I drew up there, I assume that in that area, before the war -- it is hard to say off the top of my head now, but I think there were about 30 to 40.000 Serbs living there and perhaps some 50 to 60.000 Croats. And I'm talking about this entire critical area. But I can't really give you a very precise figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if there would be areas within this circled part of the map where there would have been a large majority of Serbs, what to do -- well, let's say there may have been municipalities or towns where there was, well, let's say, up to 70 or 80 per cent, or even more of Serbs. What should the remaining 60 and 70 per cent do if they wished to return, where you had said that not ever more than 10 per cent?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I will be very specific again. They should all return, but let us settle in that area which was empty 10 per cent more of other citizens. And again I have to repeat, we always had in mind -- and when discussing these matters, we always had to think in the back of our minds we had these possibility of being attacked. But when I mean -- when I say Croats I mean citizens, ethnic Croats and ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe if could you just check -- I have line -- page 67 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. 67, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Line 1. "But let us settle in that area which is empty 10" -- something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I read part of your answer and then please correct me when there's any mistranslation. You said you will be very specific: "They should all return, but let us settle in that area which was empty 10 per cent," and then you said ... it is translated to us as "10 per cent more of other citizens." That is how it is translated to us. Is that what you said --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: No, ten times, not 10 per cent. Ten times more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten times more of the others. Now, please stay with me on arithmetics. Let's assume, original population, 70 per cent Serbs, 30 per cent Croats. Now if you want --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Not in this -- not in this area. That was not the ratio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not even in some municipalities?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I drew this circle between Una and Kupa rivers and it is my impression, if we take this whole area in consideration, that there were some 60 per cent of Croats and 40 per cent of Serbs. You know, Karlovac is a big town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 60 per cent Croats, 40 per cent Serbs. Although it may be that in some municipalities it was quite different which may have resulted in people having to remove to other parts of the area you circled. Do we agree on that? Well, let's say if in one municipality there was 80 per cent majority of Serbs. Could they then stay there, and, nevertheless, fulfil your -- or return there, and, nevertheless, fulfil your wish that there should be ten times as much Croats, as I now understand, than there were before? And some of the Serbs had to -- if we --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. If we look at a municipality as individual. But I pointed out this entire area. There is no dilemma about one or other of those municipalities in this area as being like that, but speaking of this critical area, critical for Croatia. And, again, I'm talking about the time when we still had the threat of aggression over our heads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just, for purposes of -- if we would have 40 per cent of Serbs living there, yes? Let's just, for argument's sake, assume that 50 per cent of them would wish to return, which would mean ...

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: [In English] 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, then you would need a huge amount of Croats in order to create that new situations because you wanted to have ten times as much Croats as there were before, or ten times more Croats than Serbs? I -- it is not entirely clear to me yet.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in your calculation and, of course, my profession is mathematics, you would need another hundred thousand so that you would have 120.000; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you would have a ratio of 1:6. 20 to -- no. 20 to 120 -- no. 20:140.000. I'm just trying to -- to follow your --

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. We are getting close to the figures. But please just take this with a grain of salt. We are getting closer in this math that we are trying to figure out. But this is an area that could absorb another 100.000 inhabitants because it was empty. There was no one who could work the -- till the soil or work in the woods. We still have a lot of people in Croatia who are unemployed. We have 300.000 unemployed, and this is what we were discussing rather informally. But no one ever suggested that this could all be accomplished in three days, but this was just a strategic line that was to be followed and perhaps accomplished in -- in some -- in a decade or so, or several decades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In our example we would still be well above 10 per cent, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, in the example that we gave, there would be 20.000 on the one hand, and 160.000 on the other. So some 12 per cent or so. But these are figures that we are just generally discussing here. When the president said this, he meant -- the 10 per cent, he was actually referring to the figure that was approximately the ratio of the Serb population before the war in Croatia, 10 to 12 per cent. So if our strategic direction, long-term, was in fact to retain this figure, but nowhere was it said that anyone would be prevented from going back to those areas, anyone who was prepared and wanted to be a Croatian citizen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, in order to achieve that, you would have to move people perhaps away, or would you accept that in one municipality there was still a large Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely we would accept that if that were the case. That was not in dispute at all, that we would accept a Serb majority. And second, the transfers of population is an issue which is rather open still. At that point in time we had tens of thousands of people who were refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, expelled from there, and who were waiting to be settled somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you explain this that you needed this area to be populated. Because it was empty, you said. What is at all the purpose of saying not more than 10 per cent Serbs? I mean, what you needed is population as you explained it to us. Why at all talking about what percentage could be Serb and what percentage could not be Serb? What's the use, what does it add to, apparently, what was your problem, that is, that the area should be populated?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, when I referred to a Serb, I meant those Serbs who actually took arms and fought against Croatia and did not intend to take Croatian citizenship; but when I said "Croat," I meant anyone who could be Croat or Serb or Bosnian, because there are a lot of Bosniaks in that area and hopefully some day there would be even more of them, because we needed people to develop that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's return -- could we assign a number for this marked map. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit C3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: C3 is in evidence. Can we return to -- what was it? I think we were in 463. Let me just have a look. Yes, 463. Same page where we were. That was page 10 in the English, and 14 and 15 in B/C/S. You then continue and give -- refer to certain areas, Petrova and Zrinska Gora. I do not know exactly where that is. Could you help us out? In what municipality that was, or ...

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, they were in Vojnic or Vrginmost municipality. I'm not quite sure, one of those two, close to the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, in that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said: "I'm talking about 10 per cent," and then are you pointing at various locations. And there you say you have to establish some kind of a city sooner or later. And you said: "We have also have Vojnic and Veljun, a somewhat smaller place." You say this in relation to the 10 per cent, where you focus on certain areas. How do we have to understand that you bring in other people and that, finally, the balance would be not more than 10 per cent Serbs and 90 per cent of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the map that I mentioned earlier, that was the thinking at the time. To open up that area to give incentives for people to move in, into that region rather than some other areas of Croatia. We weren't really discussing individual towns or villages or municipalities, and that they should actually change their population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you tell us, you were -- what finally was the result in this area? How many Croats were additionally -- or on from the Operation Storm? Now, you said it was approximately 60/40. Let's just assume that the 40 -- the 60 per cent Croats would remain and let's do it in terms of perhaps an example. Let's say 60.000 Croats - I'm not asking about Serbs at this moment - 40.000 Serbs. Could you tell us in -- as a result of this colonising, how many Croats are living in that area now? If you know.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figures. Unfortunately, many Croats and many Serbs did not return at all. Unfortunately. Because during their exile, they acquired new living conditions, and let's say even Croats from that area found jobs in Zagreb, in Split, in Rijeka or somewhere else, and equally numerous Serbs found jobs in Belgrade and other places. Unfortunately, thus, that area is still depopulated today. The numbers living there are insufficient. Were I in the government today, I would propose to the Croatian government a programme to stimulate life in those areas, no longer for some strategic or defence reasons but for just residence or living reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, the whole concept of colonisation was, as you explained it to us, and that's how you explained this conversation, is that by a huge import of Croats, you would have a new, if I could say so, ethnic balance, where the Croats had a 90-per cent majority.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: At the time, after Storm, it was for strategic reasons. Today I'm talking about economic reasons, and I'm generally speaking about Croatian citizens, because, for sure, there are no longer any people in Croatia who would rise up against Croatia now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, moving to page 11 in English and 17 in B/C/S, still in the same document, I read again what you stated there as we find it in the minutes. You said -- you refer to a village: "... which used to be called Maja and was predominantly Croat marked red, while the predominantly Serb areas are marked blue. It is the key area to start bringing in settlers." "Secondly, Croats are to return to Croat areas." "Thirdly, the third priority is this marked area here, the liberated Croat area, and this one here, which used to be populated by Serbs. This marked area here was populated 90 per cent by Serbs, but now it is entirely under our control. Only a few people remain." You just explained to us that you looked at the whole area, if you were thinking about settling and the balance between ethnicities. Here, apparently, you are focussing more detailed on certain areas, and you're specifically referring to 90 per cent populated -- an area populated 90 per cent by Serbs but now entirely under your control. That's at least -- but explain to me -- it sounds to me as it may be not fully consistent to say, We were just looking at the whole area; whereas, here, are you specifically looking at areas but perhaps you explain what area you exactly pointed at with a 90-per cent Serb majority which you say is "now entirely under our control."

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: We don't have video footage from that meeting to be able to see which section of the map I'm showing to the President. I would have to go over the whole transcript to refresh my recollection. But when we're saying that something is under our control, then what we mean is it was under the Croat control, the control of the Croat army and the Bosnian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think on the map we're showing a section of territory that is in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But we're not saying that we would be populating that. So it is very difficult from this segment to tell what, at that point, I was showing to the President on the map. Perhaps we could read the next page, because it's hard for me to follow the thread completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another opportunity would be to provide you with a hard copy of the transcript, so that -- I always hate to give you homework, but perhaps that you take your time to read it over and to see whether, in the context, it is -- it is -- whether you find relevant information in the context. So what you're saying here is that you may have referred here to territory not within the original borders of Croatia but, nevertheless, being under your control.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: The President refers to Kupres and Grahovo there. These are two settlements in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When we say "ours," colloquially speaking, it's -- I don't know actually to what extent it was under the control of the -- or monitoring of the Croatian army, but at the time it was under the allied friendly forces of the army of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But if the President is talking about Kupres and Grahovo here, we're talking about towns that are actually situated in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the time that I recall when the liberation of those areas from Serb occupation was under way. I think that Grahovo and Kupres -- actually, I know that for sure they were liberated before Knin was, and even that was a precondition for the liberation of other parts of Croatia. So the topic here is discussed a little bit more broadly, and it has to do with territory of a neighbouring state. And I think the context is that if there are no attacks by those attacking Croatia from the other border, then it's not so essential to have long-term defence forces on this particular side of the border, if things remain like that. I think this is what was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another document, which is D1823, which are the minutes of a closed session of the Croatian government. And there -- we do not have, I think, a front page. Page 6 in English; 11 in B/C/S. I still think we have not yet the page in English. Mr. Radic, on this page -- and let me see whether I find it in English. Maybe further down. No, it should be further up. It's at the top, line 4. You are recorded to have said -- and I think the discussion was about the draft on -- the draft decree on the -- no, let me see. Yes, the draft decree on temporary takeover and administration of specified property. You said: "It surely is a historical document, which determines, I will use the word, demographic future of the liberated areas." Could you explain us what you exactly meant by those words.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: It's hard with this sentence just taken out of context. One would need to read the whole speech to the government. But evidently, I'm talking about the fact here that in Croatia we have a large number of empty apartments and houses where we could accommodate displaced persons or exiled persons instead of placing them in hotels and other facilities. I think this is mostly relating to the property that is owned by the state or socially owned. For the most part. One would need to read the entire thing to know the context. It's hard just to be precise on the basis of one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to look at the previous page, we move to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the following one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe a contextualisation of the discussion would probably begin by Mr. Misetic on page - not this Mr. Misetic - on page 3. That's page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 3 of the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that would be in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He's talking about the issues that they are about discuss and he lays it out, that President Valentic -- or the Prime Minister Valentic gives Mr. Misetic the floor and talks about a series of individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a hard copy for you there, if you would like to quickly read the previous and the following page, then, Madam Usher, could you assist. We are talking about -- it's already there. It's D1823. Are there hard copies available to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: As for your question, what did I mean when I said strategic conditions were on what the future of the people depended on, what I meant was that for a -- it was important to return people to their homes, and I'm primarily thinking of Croats but others too, let's say those from a village, and I mentioned the village of Kijevo today, those people should be placed in empty apartments in Knin so that they could return to their houses as soon as possible. So what the strategic significance of that was, is that homes that were emptied as a result of the war would not remain empty and deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that I asked about strategic importance. I asked about how this would determine the demographic future. That is what my question was about. Because, apparently -- that's at least at first understanding of what you said, is that the draft decree on -- well, let's say the houses, whether or not to return, temporary takeover, that that would be very important for the demographic future. Now demographic future, where you told us that this legislation was aiming at preserving houses, whereas demography is, for me, different from maintenance of buildings. You say it is important for the demographic future.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: The demographic future, we adopted that programme and its first principle was that the population in Croatia be distributed throughout its territory. If you take the document, this is the first sentence of that demographic programme of ours, that the population is not concentrated only in one area but throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. But what I would like to know is what then exactly the link is between the draft, which is presented here, which is the draft decree on temporary takeover, and demography.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: The possibility for people to come to the area immediately and not to have wait for another three years before their homes can be renovated. This is most directly linked to demographics. The person from Kijevo and Kistanje, for example, would not need to wait in a hotel for another two or three years but to immediately come to their home. This is the basic demographic premise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now we earlier heard that -- or we saw that the word "pretext" was used as the aim of this type of legislation. Pretext of preservation of houses.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently there's a ... You hear me again?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about the pretext of preservation.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I'm hearing it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And here demography is -- means to you that Croats could immediately return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: These are two things that do not exclude each other but compliment each other. Thus, let's preserve the houses and bring the people close to their homesteads, so in one move one would achieve two objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't it true that this piece of legislation, whether we have the initial decree or the later law, would primarily affect Serbs who had not returned in time?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: The rule or regulation applies to them giving them a deadline by which they would need to return. But at that time there was no event that did not include everyone. Each move was interconnected. You always had one block that, if touched, would require that you also touch another block. We had to -- I'm going to add a third argument. We had to relocated Croats, for example from the Love Hotel in Trogir, in order to be able to make money during the following tourist season in that hotel, in order to use those funds to restore a house to which a Croat would return and, in turn, free up a house to which a Serb could return. So it was all interconnected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to take you -- and this will be the last document we'll look at. That's P2678. And I would like to move to page 26 in English, and 45 in B/C/S. These are the minutes of a closed session of the Croatian government, 5th of October, 1995. You are talking about: "The first priority of the overall national entity is currently to accommodate where Croatia is thinnest, and until yesterday, it was thinnest, like I said, we cannot discuss this in open session, but it was thinnest in the area south of Karlovac and up to the Slovenian border." I think that is the area we discussed before. What I'd like to know is what could not be said in -- what could not be discussed in open session?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: It was a delicate subject at the time, the one of Croats expelled from Bosnia and Herzegovina who were encouraged or incited by many when they came to Croatia that they would not be able to receive care in Croatia but that they should go wherever, from Australia to Canada. So message like that could be -- to -- understood as a disturbing one to them. We understood that there were plenty of empty state-owned and socially owned homes where people could be accommodated in that area, so it was not appropriate to pour oil on the fire or add salt to their wounds at the time when they had to run before the occupier in their countries. So -- and they didn't know what to do and where to go. So that was the reason why this was being discussed at the time, how to care for them and provide shelter to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not yet fully understand. You explained that the legislation which was drafted and the efforts were, Let's populate the areas, let's get everyone back who, at one point in time, whether Croat or Serb, would have had to leave the territory of Croatia. What was now the sensitive message? That is still unclear. Why couldn't you say, Come back, whether you were accommodated in the coast, at the coast-line or whether you had fled to other areas due to the occupation? What was the -- what couldn't you say that was so sensitive?

utterances.speaker: JURE RADIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the third group of people. I don't know if this is quite clear. People who had been expelled at that time from Bosnia-Herzegovina and to whom the message, Return immediately to your homes, under the knife of Ratko Mladic, would be -- the alternative to which would be go to Australia or Canada, and many of them did that. Unfortunately, there were plenty of empty apartments and houses in Croatia where we could have accommodated those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll re-read your answer over the break. And see whether I have any follow-up questions. Let me just see ... I would have not more than 15 minutes to conclude this examination, but rather than rushing at this moment, we'd rather do that tomorrow. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given today. It is public, but, nevertheless, you're the only one who should not speak about it. And also not about the testimony still to be given tomorrow. And we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we rise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- if I could just raise one matter, because Your Honour wanted assistance in the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we need the witness for that or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is a quick matter and if Your Honour wants to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I have another matter as well so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'd rather not bore the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the witness with that. So, therefore, you're excused at this moment. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, at 9.00, in Courtroom I. And, as I said, do not speak with anyone about your testimony. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you asked to be provided with P463. With the assistance of Chamber staff and the Usher, we'll take that out of the binder so that can you read that. It was P463, isn't, the 22nd of August ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you are already excused unless we would need the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, on that score just in the spirit of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps also D1823.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I was going to say it may be quicker certainly during the examination if the witness is given the series of transcripts that the Chamber referred to during the course of its examination. I certainly will be referring back to those, and I think it might be an easier exercise if we just give them all to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are very generous today, Mr. Radic, you can take the whole binder with you. The only matter is ... One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will not only find the exhibits we referred to but you will find your own statement as well, which you gave to the Gotovina Defence. But can you keep the binder. We expect to you bring it with you tomorrow morning. Madam Usher, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay, before we rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was just on the issue of mines which Your Honour raised with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'll -- if there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any practical way of providing us with a -- either an electronic copy or a hard copy, then perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D1813, page 29, is a passage of text in which this witness mentions the problems of de-mining. And in another exhibit, D1815, at page 11, is two passages, where -- where this witness refers to the problem of mining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you'd like us to specifically look at those pages and -- in the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it was something Your Honour raised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and you raised it with the bar as well so those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I knew there were passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that you said something about a lengthy report on de-mining is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another document which will be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's a Prosecution document that I believe has been released already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any way of giving guidance in the 61 pages so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be possible to do that, well, let's say, within the next half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, easy, yes. Yes. Not while I'm standing up at the moment because I can't remember where I've put it in this [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, then, communicate with Chambers staff on this matter so that we know, later this evening, what we have to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Any other matter? Could I inquire, the Chamber has not many questions left, a few questions in relation to the statement, which will take not more than 15 hours. As matters stand now -- oh, 15 hours. Yes. Yes, I don't know whether this is Freudian or not. As matters stand now, could the parties give an indication as to how much time they would need in cross-examination. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I anticipate approximately two sessions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two sessions. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately the same. Probably -- maybe a little bit less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two sessions. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It depends what goes before but it could be half a session to one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half a session. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The same with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which brings me to the conclusion that with a bit of discipline -- I don't know whether I've shown sufficient discipline today, but with a bit of discipline we could conclude the testimony of this witness Friday. If the parties would agree on that? It seems that the scheduling for three days seems to be more or less adequate. I would very much like to conclude the evidence by Friday and not to ask the witness to stay over for the weekend. So, therefore, the parties are urged to do their utmost best and also to find a proper balance between what is still to be asked -- I'm also looking at the Defence to see to what extent they could work together in this respect, to see whether we can conclude on Friday. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Just to forewarn the Chamber in light of the fact that there may significant -- it appears that there will be significant cross-examination by the Defence, there may be a need for the Prosecution to re-cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am aware of that. I am aware of that. Mr. Kay, you said half a session, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I said half to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half to one. Mr. Mikulicic said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It depends what goes before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the same, half to one. Let's make that three quarter then. That would mean we would need four sessions plus one and a half for the two remaining. That's five and a half sessions. We have six sessions. We will take tomorrow only 10 to 15 minutes. Therefore there would be although limited time left, and if the parties could see whether it is able to make two sessions one and three-quarters. And again the Chamber is not aiming at imposing much time-limits, but I think we all agree that, with this programme, it should be possible to conclude on Friday. We adjourn and we resume tomorrow, 9.00, Courtroom I.
